newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Amsterdam bourse offers half its shares for sale.
newsitem.headline: Amsterdam bourse offers half its shares for sale.

text.p: Amsterdam, the world's oldest bourse, moved closer to a public listing of its own shares on Thursday with the publication of a prospectus for the private placement of half its equity capital.

"This share placement represents the second step in the bourse restructuring which started with the merger of the stock exchange with the options exchange (to form Amsterdam Exchanges NV)," AEX chairman George Moeller told a news conference.
He said Amsterdam Exchanges planned to seek a public share listing in or after 2002. "We have given ourselves five years to become well-established and build up a track record," he said.
Pre-marketing for the re-offering of 50,000 "B" class, seven percent cumulative preference shares started today.

The placement will be conducted via the book-building method, whereby institutions are asked to indicate the amount of shares they want and the price they are willing to pay. ABN Amro Rothschild will act as book runner and global coordinator.
Institutional investors, issuing institutions and former exchange association members (banks and brokers) can subscribe to the offering from March 17.
Subscriptions close on March 21, and pricing and allocation of the issue will be announced on March 24.

According to the prospectus, former exchange association members will have to subscribe to at least 30 percent of the offering at an average price that is higher than that bid by institutional investors and issuing institutions.
If these two criteria are not met, no class B shares will be allocated to these subscribers.
"It can be summed up as a placement with former members and third parties, whereby preference is given to placement with third parties," Moeller said.
In addition no single shareholder will be able to own more than a 10 percent stake.
Moeller said this reflected the strategic importance of the bourse to the Dutch economy as well as the offering's aim of achieving a broad spread of ownership.
A further 50,000 "A" class seven percent cumprefs will continue to be held by members of the exchange associations which formerly owned the two bourses.
These members also hold a total of 100,000 certificates entitling them to earnings after payment of preference dividend.
Moeller said these so-called 'excess profit' certificates had a limited life of five years, and were intended to replace the end-of-year rebates paid to members under the old structure.
